references.text: Parallel passage in Matthew where Jesus asks the same question: Which is easier to say—your sins are forgiven, or to say: Get up and walk?
Parallel passage in Mark where Jesus asks the same question about what is easier to say to the paralyzed man.
Context for this verse: Jesus sees their faith and tells the paralytic that his sins are forgiven.
Continuation where Jesus proves his authority to forgive sins by commanding the paralytic to get up and walk—and the man gets up and goes home.
Jesus forgives sins on another occasion, and those present ask: Who is this who even forgives sins?—the same theme regarding Jesus' authority to forgive sins.
God is the one who blots out transgressions for his own sake and does not remember sins—Jesus' claim to forgive sins points back to the fact that only God can forgive sin.
Jesus heals a paralyzed man at the Pool of Bethesda and says: Get up, take your mat and walk—the same type of healing miracle demonstrating Jesus' divine authority.
The scribes accuse Jesus of blasphemy because only God can forgive sins—the background to Jesus' question about what is easier.
The Lord forgives all your iniquity and heals all your diseases—the connection between forgiveness and healing that Jesus demonstrates in this account.
